metadata.title: Relating teenagers’ science interest network characteristics to later science course enrolment: An analysis of Australian PISA 2006 and Longitudinal Surveys of Australian Youth data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study links Australian PISA 2006 (science literacy) to LSAY 2008 (Year 10 cohort; wave 3) and then applies exclusions to obtain a final analytic sample of 4,758 students. The manuscript does not report using PISA/LSAY sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), nor does it name any weight variable. Because the analysis is based on psychometric network estimation (bootnet/IsingFit) and subsequent regression of forecast correlations, the paper does not describe a complex-survey-weighted estimation strategy; therefore, readers should treat results as conditional on the analytic sample rather than explicitly population-representative estimates. For replication with the international databases, analysts should check the PISA/LSAY weight documentation and, if weights are available, consider whether weighted network estimation and weighted regression are feasible or whether unweighted estimation is a deliberate choice.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample was drawn from Australian PISA 2006 participants who were also followed in LSAY 2008 (wave 3) and were still in school. Students were excluded if they followed the International Baccalaureate program in their last year of secondary school (N=54) and if they were not in Year 10 in 2006 and Year 12 in 2008 to ensure the same schooling trajectory (N=611). This produced a final sample of 4,758 students (2,596 girls; 2,162 boys). For network estimation, the authors tested MCAR assumptions and then used casewise deletion of missing data.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006 (Australia) + LSAY 2008 (Year 10 cohort; Year 12 enrolment) — Chemistry course enrolment
main_findings.performance_metrics: Centrality–enrolment correlations: strength r=.36–.74 (significant, all p<.05); Chemistry strength forecast regression: F(2, 28)=20.36, p<.001, R2_adj=.56; node strength b=.76 (t(28)=6.28, p<.001) and node mean not significant b=.21 (t(28)=1.70, p=.10). Chemistry closeness forecast regression: F(2, 28)=18.58, p<.001, R2_adj=.54; node closeness b=.70 (t(28)=5.54, p<.001) and node variance b=.43 (t(28)=3.44, p=.002).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006 (Australia) linked to LSAY 2008 data for Year 10 students and their Year 12 chemistry course enrolment, the study leveraged future intentions, science enjoyment, science self-concept, and personal value centrality indicators from the science interest network model to predict chemistry enrolment, finding that both strength and closeness centrality were significant predictors (e.g., R2_adj=.56 for strength; R2_adj=.54 for closeness). This indicates that interventions targeting central motivational nodes—especially future intentions and enjoyment—may be effective levers for increasing chemistry course uptake, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006 (Australia) + LSAY 2008 (Year 10 cohort; Year 12 enrolment) — Physics course enrolment
main_findings.performance_metrics: Centrality–enrolment correlations: positive and significant for all subjects (r=.36–.74; all p<.05). Physics strength forecast regression: F(2, 28)=7.66, p=.002, R2_adj=.31; node strength b=.49 (t(28)=3.13, p=.004) and node variance not significant b=.23 (t(28)=1.48, p=.151). Physics closeness forecast regression: F(2, 28)=9.14, p<.001, R2_adj=.35; node closeness b=.52 (t(28)=3.52, p=.002) and node variance b=.43 (t(28)=2.90, p=.007).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006 (Australia) linked to LSAY 2008 data for Year 10 students and their Year 12 physics course enrolment, the study leveraged future intentions, science enjoyment, science self-concept, and personal value centrality indicators from the science interest network model to predict physics enrolment, finding that strength centrality significantly predicted enrolment (R2_adj=.31) and closeness centrality also significantly predicted enrolment (R2_adj=.35). This indicates that strengthening central motivational components—particularly future intentions and enjoyment—may support physics subject selection, while the predictive associations should not be interpreted as causal without longitudinal or experimental evidence.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006 (Australia) + LSAY 2008 (Year 10 cohort; Year 12 enrolment) — Biology course enrolment
main_findings.performance_metrics: Centrality–enrolment correlations: positive and significant for all subjects (r=.36–.74; all p<.05). Biology strength forecast regression: F(2, 29)=6.25, p=.006, R2_adj=.25; node strength b=.39 (t(29)=2.53, p=.017) and node mean b=.42 (t(29)=2.69, p=.012). Biology closeness forecast regression: F(2, 29)=6.61, p=.004, R2_adj=.27; node closeness b=.41 (t(29)=2.65, p=.013) and node mean b=.41 (t(29)=2.68, p=.012).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006 (Australia) linked to LSAY 2008 data for Year 10 students and their Year 12 biology course enrolment, the study leveraged future intentions, science enjoyment, science self-concept, and personal value centrality indicators from the science interest network model to predict biology enrolment, finding that both strength and closeness centrality were significant but with lower explained variance than chemistry and physics (R2_adj=.25 for strength; R2_adj=.27 for closeness). This indicates that motivational network centrality is still relevant for biology course uptake, but that additional or different levers may be needed to achieve stronger predictive power for biology specifically.

data.outcome_summary: The study combines Australian PISA 2006 science literacy data with LSAY 2008 (wave 3) for the 2006 cohort, following Year 10 students to their Year 12 science course enrolment decision (chemistry, physics, biology). The analytic sample is 4,758 students after excluding International Baccalaureate students and those not on the same Year 10→Year 12 trajectory; missing data were handled via casewise deletion after MCAR checks. Science knowledge indicators used PISA plausible values with PV1 for each science knowledge indicator, and all network indicators were dichotomized to improve centrality stability. Using bootnet/IsingFit psychometric network estimation, the authors found positive, significant correlations between centrality and course enrolment (r=.36–.74, all p<.05). Forecast regressions showed significant predictive relationships for both strength and closeness centrality, with the strongest explained variance for chemistry (R2_adj≈.56/.54) and physics (≈.31/.35) and weaker but significant effects for biology (≈.25/.27). Limitations include the absence of reported survey-weight use and the correlational nature of the predictive associations.
